title: My Two Friends, Turn Aside Today, or Let Me Be
intro: Al-Simma al-Qushayri asks two travelling companions to turn aside at an abandoned camp. The country he is leaving holds both a woman he loves and the evenings they once had in Najd. Al-Qali transmits a shorter set of the Rayya and Najd verses through al-Asma'i, including the reproach that it was the speaker himself who went away. In the longer ode a few words through a litter curtain, a tether biting into forelegs and a mother camel calling for her calf give separation a succession of different voices.

translation: My two friends, turn aside today, or let me be,
that we may greet the deserted traces at al-Qubayba.
1.sharh: He asks the two men to interrupt a journey for the sake of people who are gone. Greeting the bare site is a way of treating the absent as still entitled to a visit.

translation: The winds settled there and sifted away
its landmarks, leaving only slabs scattered about,
2.sharh: The winds have taken up residence where the people once lived. They winnow the site until the heavy stones alone can mark it.

translation: and three stones in the camp, as though they were
three pigeons perched facing one another.
3.sharh: The three supports once held a cooking pot above the fire. Blackened by smoke and arranged in a ring, they look like birds at rest.

translation: Was it for a home at the two peaks of al-Raqashayn,
where summer winds swept through time and again,
4.sharh: The question leaves the tears unnamed for a whole verse. First we see the two heights and the winds repeatedly crossing the same patch of ground.

translation: that your left eye wept, and when you checked it
for such folly after composure, both eyes streamed together?
5.sharh: He tries to restore adult composure by rebuking one eye. The other joins in, so the attempt at discipline doubles the visible grief.

translation: I saw no one like the woman of Amir before her,
nor since, for saying goodbye the day we moved away.
6.sharh: He compares her with everyone he has had to leave. The test he chooses is the all-too-brief business of saying goodbye.

translation: On parting morning she showed a young gazelle's eye
and a gazelle's long neck encircled with necklaces.
7.sharh: Her jewellery belongs to the human figure, but it frames a gazelle's long neck. An eye and a movement of the head suffice to recall the woman who was leaving.

translation: Even the mother of a fawn with two dark stripes,
among the ripe arak of al-A'raf, close within reach,
8.sharh: The dark stripes belong to the fawn. The arak is close enough for the doe to browse, and its fruit is ripe. Another two verses will pass before the speaker tells us whom she resembles.

translation: who rose from over him and shook off the dew
when she saw the sun’s brow rise clear,
9.sharh: The doe rises from over her fawn, carrying a little of the night away in the dew on her. The first edge of the sun has cleared the horizon.

translation: was no lovelier than Umm al-Muhayya, glimpsed unawares,
when her neck appeared at the edge of the curtain.
10.sharh: The wait for the comparison's end measures how brief his glimpse of the woman was. Its frame is the edge of a litter curtain.

translation: When we snatched what scraps of her talk we could,
hurriedly, and a softness in her glance gave hope,
11.sharh: Conversation is broken up into little prizes seized in haste. What her eyes allow them to hope matters as much as the incomplete words.

translation: she sprinkled us with words that almost healed the ache,
holding our hearts together lest they split,
12.sharh: What she says arrives in drops. The seat of feeling in the Arabic is the liver, an organ her words seem physically to keep from breaking up.

translation: as a thirsty man sips the drops left by a cloud,
a scattering of rain whose downpour has withdrawn.
13.sharh: A thirsty man has arrived in time for the last scattered drops. There was much more in the cloud, just as there was more the lovers might have said.

translation: I told her what a hold her people had on my heart
and how I feared the gathered clan would scatter.
14.sharh: His feeling for her gives the whole encampment a hold on him. If its people strike their tents and part, he may lose even these few moments with her. The collected diwan describes the grip of love between the two.

translation: She spoke to me only in a broken answering sound.
Her two eyes brimmed, ready to spill.
15.sharh: He strains to hear an answer and receives scarcely more than a catch in the voice. The gathering tears disclose what the words have failed to finish.

translation: As though parting were something you'd never seen before her,
as though no loved companion's loss had ever struck you.
16.sharh: He has survived other farewells. The reproach he addresses to himself shows how little practice has done to prepare him for this one.

translation: If only the clan's camels, on the day they moved,
had reached evening at Dhu Salam worn out and lame,
17.sharh: His wish attacks the departure at its means of transport. Evening might have found the mounts too tired and lame to carry the camp farther away.

translation: so morning found them unable to walk with a rider
or travel through Najd, however broad the road.
18.sharh: He carries the wish into the following morning. Ideally even a broad, easy track would fail to get the riders away.

translation: You grieve while the two clans have yet to separate.
What then when the herald makes them hear the call to part?
19.sharh: He catches himself grieving in advance. The herald's audible call will turn a private apprehension into a public departure.

translation: I went on. Had I made the ache in me heard
by one worn-out caravan camel, it would have yearned and cried back.
20.sharh: A spent animal at the end of its strength would still find a voice to answer his grief. The caravan begins to sound with something more than the riders' voices.

translation: You two ravens at her tent, do not rise apart.
Fly together with longing and alight together.
21.sharh: Ravens carry the association of a caravan's departure. He tries to govern the omen by insisting that the birds must stay together in flight and on landing.

translation: Do you cry for Rayya, when you yourself put distance
between you and Rayya while your two clans were together?
22.sharh: The repeated name holds her still while the responsibility for distance shifts to him. He went away when it was still possible to remain close.

translation: It's scarcely fair to undertake a thing freely
then despair when the call of longing rings out.
23.sharh: Two calls now contend for him. The public summons to leave has had its answer, but longing has a voice of its own.

translation: As though you had never watched a traveller say farewell
or seen the two branches of a friendship pulled apart.
24.sharh: He has witnessed other friends' lives separating. Recollecting their goodbyes does nothing to make his own look ordinary.

translation: My people struck camp at Qanin and left behind
Layla's people, as good rain fell and pasture flourished.
25.sharh: The same rain favours those who stay behind as his people move away. The singer calls the woman Layla here. Al-Jabr's text names Rayya and gives the place as Qani.

translation: My two friends, who have agreed
to go on blaming me until I yield and bow,
26.sharh: The two companions of the opening have reached an agreement of their own. He hears their advice as pressure to surrender.

translation: stop. I must turn and look once more,
a long searching look, whether the people be scattered or together.
27.sharh: He delays the departure by exactly the length of one backward look. It will have to serve whether he can pick out a group or only scattered figures.

translation: I have found that blame never drives love away.
Despair, I find, offers more help and does more good
28.sharh: Scolding has been tried and found useless. He reaches for the harsher remedy of having no hope left to feed his desire.

translation: to a man whose people have wrested his own affairs from him,
who hides a tear for shame of being seen.
29.sharh: Others have taken the choice from him. The one thing over which he can still try to exercise control is whether they see his tear.

translation: His grief and memories stir whenever
he hums a tune or gains a height above the land.
30.sharh: A tune can do it, or the sudden view from rising ground. Memory needs very little help in overtaking a traveller.

translation: Stop. Say farewell to Najd and those dwelling in the Hima.
To give Najd a farewell is little enough from us.
31.sharh: He asks the companions to say goodbye to an entire region. Even that courtesy seems to him a small repayment for what they have had there.

translation: I'd give my life for that land. How sweet its hills,
how lovely the places for summer and for spring.
32.sharh: His praise follows the seasons through their different camping places. What he wishes for is enough time on this land to enjoy the turn between them.

translation: I remember the days of the Hima, then double over
my aching liver, afraid it will split.
33.sharh: In this poetry the liver can be the body's seat of grief. He bends over as though he could keep the organ from splitting by holding it in.

translation: The evenings of the Hima will never come back
to you. Let both your eyes shed tears.
34.sharh: The opening rebuke to his weeping eye has run its course. Since he cannot call back the evenings, he can at least release the tears.

translation: With me is every untried youth who has defied his critics
to meet fair women since the day he grew tall.
35.sharh: The companions belong to a remembered time when defying a warning seemed as easy as growing up. Love came before long experience of its costs.

translation: When one walks out wearing his two wraps,
all watching eyes hurry to follow him.
36.sharh: There is no elaborate description of the youth's looks. The watchers' inability to look slowly tells us what his appearance does.

translation: In a company like a herd I saw fair young women.
Ask them for a meeting, and they break off all contact.
37.sharh: The young women are first seen as a graceful group. Requesting a closer connection brings the sharp opposite of connection, a clean break.

translation: They walked in a gentle current, like running water.
Watching their swaying steps, you'd think their feet were lame.
38.sharh: The water suggests an unbroken file, though al-Jabr also allows that they are walking alongside its course. Their individual steps sway so slowly they seem to limp.

translation: I said, “May God water the Hima with lasting rain.”
They said, “May God give you steeped poison to drink.”
39.sharh: The women keep both his blessing's verb and its invocation of God. By changing what is poured, they turn a wish for life into a curse.

translation: I said, “Peace be upon you. I find
nothing this side of the Hima to satisfy me today.”
40.sharh: He persists in courtesy after the curse. The declaration that follows stakes his truthfulness on what the protected pasture means to him.

translation: They said, “If you are lying, may God show you
the fingers of your right hand cut off.”
41.sharh: Their answer makes the oath costly only if his claim is false. He is made to imagine looking at his own right hand to learn the result.

translation: When I saw al-Bishr stretch across our way
and the daughters of longing roamed, crying to go back,
42.sharh: Al-Bishr comes across his line of sight. The impulses he calls longing's daughters give voice like animals yearning to return.

translation: I looked back toward the camp until I felt
the front and side of my neck aching from the tilt.
43.sharh: The body measures how long he has kept looking back. He can locate the ache at the front of his neck and along the side.

translation: If you truly expect my love to pass
and us to drink our fill and slake this thirst,
44.sharh: He grants the hope for the length of a sentence. In this reading, also quoted by al-Qali, what would finally quench him is a drink. Al-Jabr prints “youth.”

translation: then turn back the blowing wind, or change the ache
once it takes shelter deep inside and holds its ground.
45.sharh: They may try their strength first on a wind already blowing. Longing has found cover in his body and will be at least as hard to dislodge.

translation: By God's majesty, if you remembered me
as I remember you, you could never check your tears.
46.sharh: He has only his own memory of her as a measure of her thoughts. The tears he says she could never hold back invite the answer in her own voice.

translation: She said, “Yes, by God. Mine is a remembrance that,
poured over solid rock, would split it open.”
47.sharh: She accepts the test of force and supplies a stronger material. What she feels could do to stone what he expected to see in another person's eyes.

translation: A creature longs for its highland home and cries out,
sick of the water and grazing of al-Shara and the lowlands.
48.sharh: The thirsty traveller's vocabulary changes to that of pasture. This creature has water and forage at hand, but its desire belongs to higher country.

translation: High on al-Shara, beyond reach, it saw
the paths from Najd and the open land, and cried again.
49.sharh: From the height it can see a way toward home and give voice. Al-Jabr restores this connecting view from al-Hamdani's description of Arabia.

translation: The biting tether stirred its longing. It sickened of
its grazing between a rocky rise and a sweep of sand.
50.sharh: The tether bites just where a first step would make escape possible. It is confinement that makes the present grazing unendurable.

translation: It reached with its eyes for the high mountains,
for what no tethered creature can hope to reach.
51.sharh: Its eyes travel the whole distance. The mountains only look attainable while it can forget the much shorter reach of its forelegs.

translation: Whenever it sought a way up, its course was checked
by a stoutly twisted rope that bit painfully into both forelegs.
52.sharh: Now we feel the construction of the tether itself. Its plies hold so securely that the animal's effort comes back to it as pain in the forelegs.

translation: Its longing was no greater than mine for Rayya
the morning the herald called out that we must part.
53.sharh: Only now does the sentence give us the measure to which the tethered creature is being compared. It is a single morning and a human voice announcing departure.

translation: Nor was a young camel’s, when she saw
fresh drag marks and where her first calf had fallen.
54.sharh: The young camel has lost her first calf. Like the speaker at the beginning, she has only marks on the ground from which to recognise the absent one.

translation: When, late in the night, she repeats a yearning cry
at this fresh memory, she makes all the old camels weep.
55.sharh: The loss has scarcely had time to become a memory. Even the oldest animals in the herd answer a young mother's voice.

translation: I fear that after her my spirit will find satisfaction
in nothing in this world, however much it ought to suffice.
56.sharh: He has described animals for whom the necessities of life are insufficient. He is afraid of coming to live in precisely that condition himself.

translation: I scold my soul for loving her now we are kept apart.
Still it insists on looking longingly that way.
57.sharh: He now speaks to himself much as the two friends spoke to him. The longing look survives as the last action no one can prevent.

translation: Farewell to the world. What ease can it give
if my life and yours are never brought together?
58.sharh: The farewell widens from a camp and a country to the world itself. What could make any part of it habitable is the chance of being together.

translation: No welcome to a campsite you do not inhabit,
even one lush with grass and wet along its edges.
59.sharh: He imagines the kind of damp, green campsite travellers normally seek out. Their absence is enough to cancel every one of its advantages.

translation: Water without grazing, or grazing without water,
and where I find both, a haunt of wild beasts.
60.sharh: Each apparent solution lacks a condition of life. The one place where water and pasture coincide is the very place where a traveller cannot rest in safety.

translation: By my life, the herald of our parting has called
for us to be scattered through every valley, and made himself heard.
61.sharh: The call that once reached two encampments now seems to carry through every valley. One voice has produced a multitude of different destinations.

translation: As though we were created for distance, as though
the days themselves were forbidden to bring us together.
62.sharh: He makes separation sound almost like a law imposed on time. The twice-repeated “as though” lets us hear the human weariness behind so vast a claim.

1.1.2.head: عاجَ
1.1.2.meaning: Turn off your road and stop for a while, addressed to two companions.

1.2.3.head: القُبَيبَة
1.2.3.meaning: Al-Qubayba, the place named in the opening also transmitted by Usama ibn Munqidh. Its location is uncertain.

1.2.4.head: بَلقَع
1.2.4.meaning: A stretch of land deserted by its inhabitants.

2.1.1.head: أَرَبَّ
2.1.1.meaning: Stayed persistently in one place, here of the winds.

2.2.3-4.head: الصَّفيح المُوَضَّع
2.2.3-4.meaning: Broad stone slabs lying here and there about the camp.

3.1.2.head: ثَلاث
3.1.2.meaning: The three hearthstones set around the fire to support a cooking pot.

3.2.4.head: وُقَّع
3.2.4.meaning: Birds that have settled or alighted.

4.2.4-5.head: بَدءاً وَرُجَّعاً
4.2.4-5.meaning: First coming, then returning time and again.

5.1.2-3.head: العَين اليُسرى
5.1.2-3.meaning: He addresses his left eye in the second person here. Al-Qali gives “my left eye.” Other tellings name the right.

5.2.5.head: أَسبَلَ
5.2.5.meaning: The two eyes let their tears fall in an unbroken stream.

6.1.4.head: العامِرِيَّة
6.1.4.meaning: The woman of Banu Amir, identified by al-Jabr with Rayya later in the poem.

7.1.4-5.head: مُقلَة شادِن
7.1.4-5.meaning: The eye of a young gazelle grown strong enough to do without its mother.

7.2.5.head: أَتلَع
7.2.5.meaning: Long-necked, here of the neck on which the necklaces hang.

8.1.3-4.head: أَحوى الجُدَّتَين
8.1.3-4.meaning: A fawn with a pair of dark stripes along its back.

8.2.1.head: أَراك
8.2.1.meaning: Arak, a desert tree browsed by gazelles, whose twigs serve as tooth sticks.

8.2.3.head: الأَعراف
8.2.3.meaning: High ground, identified by Hamad al-Jasir as the heights of Lubna. The name also occurs elsewhere.

8.2.4.meaning: Came near, within the doe’s reach. The diwan has ajna, “bore fruit ready to gather.” The two verbs are close in this recording.

9.1.5.head: الطَّلّ
9.1.5.meaning: The fine dew left on bodies and plants overnight.

9.2.2-3.head: حاجِب الشَّمس
9.2.2-3.meaning: The upper rim as the sun clears the horizon.

10.1.3-4.head: أُمّ المُحَيّا
10.1.3-4.meaning: The beloved's name by kunya here, understood by al-Jabr as Rayya.

10.2.4-5.head: كِفَّة السِّتر
10.2.4-5.meaning: The hem of the riding litter's curtain, where her neck comes into view.

11.1.3-4.head: سِقاط الحَديث
11.1.3-4.meaning: Scraps of speech snatched before the chance of conversation goes by.

11.2.1.head: غِشاش
11.2.1.meaning: Hastily, with little time to spare.

12.1.6.meaning: The inward burning of consuming love.

12.1.4.head: شَفى
12.1.4.meaning: Her words almost heal him. The diwan uses the passive verb, so that the lover is the one who is almost healed.

12.2.3.head: كَبِد
12.2.3.meaning: Livers, understood as a seat of intense feeling much as English speaks of an aching heart.

13.1.4-5.head: وَقائِع مُزنَة
13.1.4-5.meaning: Drops fallen from a rain-bearing cloud.

14.1.3-4.head: ضَبثَة الحَيّ
14.1.3-4.meaning: “The grip of the camp,” the hold its people have on his heart. The diwan has “the grip of love between us.”

14.2.2-3.head: شَعب الحَيّ
14.2.2-3.meaning: The community of the camp, bound by kinship or shared residence.

15.1.4.head: رَجع
15.1.4.meaning: An answering sound that falters as speech shades into weeping.

16.2.3.head: أُلّاف
16.2.3.meaning: Familiar companions and ones dearly loved.

17.2.1-2.head: ذو سَلَم
17.2.1-2.meaning: Dhu Salam, one of several places bearing the name. Its precise location here is disputed.

17.2.4-5.head: مَزاحيف ظُلَّع
17.2.4-5.meaning: Camels so exhausted that they shuffle and limp.

18.2.7.head: مَهيَع
18.2.7.meaning: A broad track that ordinarily offers easy passage.

19.1.2.head: حَيّ
19.1.2.meaning: The two encamped groups about to take different routes.

20.2.1-2.head: رَذِيّ قِطار
20.2.1-2.meaning: A spent camel from a file of animals strung together.

21.1.3-4.head: غُرابا البَيت
21.1.3-4.meaning: Two ravens by her tent in the recitation. The diwan's “ravens of her parting” invokes a bird taken as an omen of separation.

22.1.1.head: بَكى
22.1.1.meaning: A question turned back on himself. Al-Asma'i's excerpt in the Amali opens “You yearned for Rayya.”

22.1.3.meaning: Rayya, the beloved in the widely transmitted Najd passage.

22.2.1.head: مَزار
22.2.1.meaning: The place one visits, or the act of visiting.

24.2.3-4.head: شَعبا صاحِبَين
24.2.3-4.meaning: The joined lives or branches of two friends. The root can express both joining and dividing.

25.1.4.head: قَنين
25.1.4.meaning: Qanin in the performance. Al-Jabr prints Qani and cites al-Jasir on the unstable transmission of the place-name.

25.2.3.meaning: Here he says Layla. Al-Jabr has “Rayya's people,” agreeing with the name elsewhere.

25.2.5-6.head: جيدَ وَأَمرَعَ
25.2.5-6.meaning: The place received generous rain and grew lush with pasture.

26.2.5.head: ضَرَعَ
26.2.5.meaning: Yield or humble myself before the two friends.

27.2.1.head: مُصَعَّدَة
27.2.1.meaning: A lingering, searching look, also suggesting the eyes being raised.

29.1.3-5.meaning: His people overruled him and took the decision into their hands.

30.2.6.head: مَيفَع
30.2.6.meaning: A height that commands a view of its surroundings.

31.1.6.head: الحِمى
31.1.6.meaning: The reserved pasture, here the country of Najd he associates with Rayya.

31.1.5.meaning: Settled or camped. The opening consonant sounds like the plain h of halla in this performance. The farewell in the early sources uses the verb for settling in a place.

32.2.3-4.head: المُصطاف وَالمُتَرَبَّع
32.2.3-4.meaning: The summer encampment and the spring grazing camp.

35.1.3.head: غِرّ
35.1.3.meaning: A youth with little experience of the world.

35.2.2.head: غانِيَة
35.2.2.meaning: Beautiful women, traditionally explained as women whose beauty makes adornment unnecessary.

36.1.5.head: رِداء
36.1.5.meaning: The two wraps worn by the youth as he walks out.

37.1.1.head: سِرب
37.1.1.meaning: A herd of gazelles, a term transferred to a company of women.

37.2.2.head: سامَ
37.2.2.meaning: Proposed or sought a meeting with them.

39.1.5-6.head: دِيَم الحَيا
39.1.5-6.meaning: Gentle, lasting rains that bring the land to life.

40.2.6.head: مَقنَع
40.2.6.meaning: Something that would give satisfaction or suffice.

41.2.1.head: بَنان
41.2.1.meaning: Fingertips. The threat extends to his hand.

42.1.3.head: البِشر
42.1.3.meaning: Al-Bishr, a landmark intervening between the traveller and the camp.

42.2.2-3.head: بَنات الشَّوق
42.2.2-3.meaning: “Daughters of longing,” the impulses born of yearning, given living voices.

43.2.4-5.head: ليت وَأَخدَع
43.2.4-5.meaning: The front of the neck and a vein along its side, strained by continual turning.

44.2.3.head: الشَّراب
44.2.3.meaning: Drink. Al-Riyashi's version in the Amali supports the recitation. Al-Jabr prints “youth.”

45.2.3-4.head: أَلواذ الحَشا
45.2.3-4.meaning: The recesses and sheltered places of the body's interior.

46.2.5.head: أَدمُع
46.2.5.meaning: Tears. The collected diwan has a singular expression, madma'an.

47.2.3-4.head: الصَّخر الأَصَمّ
47.2.3-4.meaning: Solid rock. The diwan has “the hardest of the smooth rocks.”

48.1.3-4.head: عِلوِيّ الهَوى
48.1.3-4.meaning: One whose longing is for the highlands, pictured in the next verses held back by a tether.

48.1.6.head: اِجتَوى
48.1.6.meaning: Found a place uncongenial and could take no pleasure in living there.

48.2.2.meaning: Al-Shara. Several places bear the name. Al-Hamdani quotes the next verse in identifying a mountain.

49.2.1-2.head: مَصادِر نَجد
49.2.1-2.meaning: The ways out toward Najd. Al-Hamdani quotes the verse individually under the name al-Qushayri.

50.2.4.head: قُفّ
50.2.4.meaning: A rise of hard, stony ground.

50.2.5.head: أَجرَع
50.2.5.meaning: Sandy ground or a dune with a sandy flank.

52.1.6.head: شَأو
52.1.6.meaning: The goal or reach of its course.

52.2.1-2.head: أَمين القُوى
52.2.1-2.meaning: A dependable tether. Its strength lies in the plies twisted together.

54.1.2-3.head: بَكرَة بِكر
54.1.2-3.meaning: A young she-camel with her first calf.

54.2.1.head: مَجَرّ
54.2.1.meaning: A drag mark on the ground.

55.2.4.head: بازِل
55.2.4.meaning: Mature camels whose permanent canine teeth have come through.

57.2.2.meaning: Toward the object of his longing. The diwan has the explicitly feminine “toward her.”

58.2.4.head: شَمل
58.2.4.meaning: The shared life and company that bind a person to loved ones.

59.2.3-4.head: مُخضَلّ الجَوانِب
59.2.3-4.meaning: Wet along the edges with rain or dew.

60.2.5.head: مَسبَع
60.2.5.meaning: A place frequented by predatory animals.

61.2.1.head: تَشتيت
61.2.1.meaning: For our scattering. The diwan instead speaks of our scattered company.

62.1.3.head: النَّوى
62.1.3.meaning: For distance and separation from home and loved ones.

62.2.5.head: تَجَمَّعَ
62.2.5.meaning: Come together again. The reciter speaks in the first person plural. Al-Jabr prints the verb without its initial n.
